identity.title: Protein Fold Classification at Scale: Benchmarking and Pretraining

problem.claim: Protein topology/fold classification is needed to help decipher biological function.

gap.claim: Progress is limited by a lack of large-scale duplicate-avoiding benchmarks and by protein-classification models that do not scale well.

contributions.claim: Introduces TEDBench, a large-scale non-redundant protein fold-classification benchmark built from TED and Foldseek-clustered AlphaFold structures.

Proposes Masked Invariant Autoencoders (MiAE), a self-supervised structure-representation framework combining up to 90% masking, an SE(3)-invariant encoder, and a lightweight coordinate-reconstructing decoder.
Benchmarks transfer beyond AlphaFold structures using a curated dataset of experimental CATH v4.4 structures.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present TEDBench and MiAE as a benchmark-and-pretraining recipe for scalable protein fold classification.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that existing protein representation-learning methods on TEDBench either require very large models or fail to achieve strong performance.
The authors report that MiAE scales well and outperforms supervised counterparts and state-of-the-art baselines on TEDBench.
The authors report an additional transfer benchmark using experimental structures from CATH v4.4, but the abstract gives no result for it.

narrative_sequence.summary: Protein topology classification matters for biological-function analysis, but benchmark scale, duplicate control, and model scaling are limiting factors.
The paper introduces TEDBench as a large-scale, non-redundant benchmark derived from TED and Foldseek-clustered AlphaFold structures.
It proposes MiAE, using extreme masking, SE(3)-invariant encoding, and lightweight reconstruction of backbone coordinates.
The authors report strong TEDBench performance against supervised and state-of-the-art baselines, then test transfer on experimental CATH v4.4 structures.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns a newly defined benchmark with a pretraining method and then reports comparisons on that benchmark before adding an out-of-distribution structure-source check.

lessons.interpretation: This creates a compact claim-evidence chain connecting evaluation design, method choice, and transfer scope.
lessons.application: When introducing a representation-learning method, pair a clearly specified benchmark with direct baseline comparisons and a second evaluation source that tests whether gains depend on the original data pipeline.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when no meaningful independent data source or task-specific benchmark can be constructed.

unknowns: TEDBench size, split protocol, duplicate criteria, and evaluation metrics are unspecified.
The abstract does not provide quantitative results, model sizes, computational costs, or the outcome of the CATH v4.4 transfer benchmark.
The abstract does not establish independently verified correctness, effectiveness, reproducibility, or priority of the stated contributions.
